response.query: How should we simulate power for a three-wave multilevel growth model with nested clusters (students in schools/counties), what software or code to use, and what power thresholds justify oversampling?
response.answer: To simulate power for a three-wave multilevel growth model, use software like R with the "lme4" package or Mplus. Aim for an ICC above 0.10 and a power threshold of 0.80 for adequate oversampling.

results.title: Frontiers | Adequate Sample Sizes for a Three-Level Growth Model
results.content: When researchers conduct a three-level growth model analysis, the question of sufficient sample size for adequate statistical power and accurate estimates of parameters arise. In this paper, simulation studies are used to examine the effects of different sample sizes at each level on the accurate estimates and adequate power in three-level growth models in which time points are nested within individuals and individuals are nested within groups. The purpose of this paper was to perform simulation studies for three-level growth models and to illustrate the effect of the ICC, level-2 and level-3 sample size on the accuracy of estimates and power. As previously researched, standard error estimates of group-level variance are the most influenced model estimate when the sample size is small (Maas and Hox, 2005; Clarke, 2008). This study indicates that required sample sizes can be different, according to researchers' interest in parameter estimates (i.e., fixed effect, random effect) at each level, ICC and statistical power.

results.title: Multilevel model - Wikipedia
results.content: A random slopes model is a model in which slopes are allowed to vary according to a correlation matrix, and therefore, the slopes are different across grouping variable such as time or individuals. Statistical power for multilevel models differs depending on whether it is level 1 or level 2 effects that are being examined. The issue of statistical power in multilevel models is complicated by the fact that power varies as a function of effect size and intraclass correlations, it differs for fixed effects versus random effects, and it changes depending on the number of groups and the number of individual observations per group. Multilevel models are a subclass of hierarchical Bayesian models, which are general models with multiple levels of random variables and arbitrary relationships among the different variables. results.title: mixed model - Under what conditions should one use multilevel/hierarchical analysis? - Cross Validated
results.content: When the structure of your data is naturally hierarchical or nested, multilevel modeling is a good candidate. A popular and good book to start with is Gelman's *Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierachical Models*. Multi-level modelling is appropriate, as the name suggests, when your data have influences occurring at different levels (individual, over time, over domains, etc). The efficiency and stable parameter estimates of HB models becomes really important when you have sparse data (e.g., less no of obs than the no of parameters at the individual level) and when you want to estimate individual level estimates. * $\begingroup$ From an analytical perspective HB analysis = multi-level models. Multi-level models should be employed when the data are nested in a hierarchical structure, particularly when there are significant differences between higher level units in the dependent variable (e.g., student achievement orientation varies between students, and also between the classes with which the students are nested).
